claim: Gligoric 2015 (Ekstazi): selecting tests by dynamic file dependencies cut end-to-end testing time 32% on average against running all tests, and 54% on longer-running suites, over 615 revisions of 32 open-source projects.
note: Gain is per check run; it holds only for suites that take over about a minute.

claim: Gligoric 2015 (Ekstazi): selection was slower than running all tests on projects with short test suites, by 9% to 138% (slowdown), and on suites over a minute it roughly halved testing time on average.
Gligoric 2015 (Ekstazi): on the Cucumber project Ekstazi selected 12% of test entities on average but took 99% of the RetestAll time.
note: One project; a selection that is small in count can still save little time.

claim: Elbaum 2014: pre-submit selection by failure and execution windows (Wf = 96) detected 70% to 80% of failing test suites at Google, and random selection of the same number of suites was about six times worse at detecting failures (3.5 million suite executions over 30 days).
note: The window setting Wf = 96 is the paper's best; the 20% to 30% not selected are delayed to post-submit, not lost.

claim: Elbaum 2014: with a 0.5% suite failure rate and 33% of suites selected pre-submit, the suites moved to post-submit added less than 0.17% of the pre-submit testing load.
note: Assumes the 0.5% failure rate of the paper's dataset and does not model infrastructure availability.

claim: Machalica 2019 (self-reported, Facebook): predictive test selection cut total infrastructure test cost by a factor of two and test executions by a factor of three against selection by build dependencies, while over 95% of individual test failures and over 99.9% of faulty changes were still reported, in production at Facebook's mobile repository.
note: Self-reported production figures, uncontrolled; the classifier was trained on three months of per-test outcomes.

claim: Machalica 2019 (self-reported, Facebook): the predictive selection picked fewer than a third of the tests that selection by build dependencies would pick.
Machalica 2019: training the predictive classifier on flaky test results gave very poor predictions.

Kondareddy 2025 (self-reported, Google): speculative cycles cut the median (p50) time to detect novel breaking targets by about 65%, from 107 to 37 minutes, over three months of production data (120 billion test-cycle pairs, 7.7 million breaking targets).
note: Self-reported production figures at Google, with a very large test history; it speeds detection and does not shorten one run.

claim: Kondareddy 2025 (self-reported, Google): with a budget of 25% of the total targets, transition prediction reached 85% recall of breakages.
Kondareddy 2025 (self-reported, Google): a test broken by a developer's change took 1 to 2 hours to start failing in TAP post-submit.

Fallahzadeh 2023: constant batch size 4 kept the actual average feedback time with up to 72% fewer machines, and gave a constant execution reduction of up to 75%, in simulation over recorded histories.
note: Simulation on Ericsson integration data (over 11,000 changes in six weeks) and Chrome (276 million test outcomes, build failure rate about 8.5%); no test was re-run; a batch fails if any included build failed.

claim: Fallahzadeh 2023: BatchAll kept the actual average feedback time with up to 91% fewer machines, in simulation over recorded histories.
note: Same simulation as x33-0311; batch size taken from queue length.

claim: Fallahzadeh 2023: the effect of adding test machines on feedback time is non-linear, because each test's delay compounds across the whole test queue.
Luo 2014: of 161 classified flaky-test fix commits, 45% were async wait, 20% concurrency and 12% test order dependency (out of 201 studied, 40 hard to classify).
note: The shares are of the 161 classified commits, not of all 201; the source is a course-site copy of the ACM paper.

claim: Luo 2014: Google's practice, as the paper states it, reruns a failing test 10 times against the same code version and labels it flaky if any rerun passes.
note: A procedure as stated in the paper, not a measured figure.

claim: Schwendner 2025 (self-reported, BMW): after Bazel affected-target selection had already been applied, pre-submit and post-submit pipelines still took 34 and 56 minutes, and 58% of test targets failed in post-submit.
note: Company's own monorepo; the 58% figure is post-submit only.

claim: Schwendner 2025 (self-reported, BMW): at a 50% time budget the prioritiser detected over 87% of transitions immediately and over 98% within three CI cycles, on the company's own history.
note: Results sections were read by search, not in full; a summary-level figure, not for a decision until the results section is read.

claim: Schwendner 2025 (self-reported, BMW): at a 20% time budget the CostChangeRank found 25.43% of relevant transitions against 20.69% for random ordering, on the company's own history.
note: Gap against random is small; results sections were read by search, not in full.

claim: Mossige 2017: random test-to-machine assignment was 30% to 60% worse than greedy scheduling, on synthetic suites built from three real suites of 33 to 132 tests.
note: Weak evidence: synthetic suites, known durations, no single gain figure; greedy is beaten only by a margin on hard instances.

claim: Mossige 2017: TC-Sched scheduled 500 test cases over 100 machines in under 4 minutes for 99.5% of its instances.
note: Instance set is synthetic; the timing is for the scheduler alone, on hardware not stated in the collect file.

claim: Memon 2017 (self-reported, Google): the compute cost of testing each change grew quadratically, as the product of the code submission rate and the size of the test pool, at more than 13K projects, 800K builds and 150 million test runs per average day.
note: Company's own account of its system; uncontrolled figures.

claim: Memon 2017 (self-reported, Google): a milestone was cut about every 45 minutes at peak development time, could hold up to 4.2 million tests, and caused delays of up to 9 hours.
note: Company's own account; the delay is the lag of a batched cycle.

claim: Memon 2017 (self-reported, Google): the ratio of passed to failed test targets per code change was 99:1, and only 1.23% of targets found a real breakage or fix after flaky targets were removed.
note: Company's own figures on its own dataset; most targets never fail, so most runs are not breakage finders.

claim: Memon 2017 (self-reported, Google): in a simulation over the studied Feb 11 to Mar 11, 2016 window, running only targets within MinDist 10 or 6 runs 61% and 50% of test targets, saved 42% and 55% of resources, and missed no breakage or fix.
note: Simulation on Google's history, not a live trial; baseline is running every affected target at every affecting change.

claim: Memon 2017 (self-reported, Google): with batched milestones, any of the N changes between the last pass and the failure may have caused a breakage, so a failed batch leaves a culprit search.
note: Stated in the paper's text at its milestone discussion; the collect file cites the lines of the saved copy.
